content:
One of the world's most popular games, played by millions of people worldwide, chess is a board game between two players. It is sometimes called international chess or Western chess to distinguish it from related games, such as “xiangqi” (Chinese chess) and “shogi” (Japanese chess). Chess is an abstract strategy game and involves no hidden information. It is played on a chessboard with 64 squares arranged in an eight-by-eight grid. At the start, each player controls sixteen pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. The player controlling the white pieces moves first, followed by the player controlling the black pieces. The object of the game is to checkmate the opponent's king, whereby the king is under immediate attack (in "check"), and there is no way for it to escape. There are also several ways a game can end in a draw.

Chess as it’s known today evolved in Spain and Southern Europe during the latter half of the 15th century. This was after evolving from ‘chaturanga,’ a similar but much older game of Indian origin. There are many predecessor games, however. The earliest texts referring to the origins of chess date from the beginning of the 7th century. Three are written in ‘Pahlavi’ (Middle Persian). Another, the ‘Harshacharita,’ is in Sanskrit. One of these texts, the ‘Chatrang-namak,’ represents one of the earliest written accounts of chess. The oldest known chess manual was in Arabic and dates to about 840. It was written by al-Adli ar-Rumi (800–870), a renowned Arab chess player, and titled ‘Kitab ash-shatranj’ (The Book of Chess). This is a lost manuscript, but it is mentioned in later works. By the twentieth century, a substantial consensus developed regarding chess's origins in northwest India in the early 7th century.

The early forms of chess in India were known as "chaturaṅga," literally meaning "four divisions" of the military: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariotry. These were represented by pieces that would become the modern pawn, knight, bishop, and rook, respectively. "Chaturanga" was played on an 8×8 uncheckered board, called "ashtāpada." From there, it spread eastward and westward along the Silk Road. The earliest evidence of chess is found in the nearby Sasanian Persia around 600 BCE, where the game was called "chatrang." The Muslim world took up Chatrang after the Islamic conquest of Persia (633–51). Then it was named "shatranj." In Spanish, "shatranj" was rendered as ajedrez ("al-shatranj"), in Portuguese as xadrez, and in Greek as zatrikion. In the rest of Europe, it was replaced by versions of the Persian "shāh" ("king"), from which the English words "check" and "chess" descend. The word "checkmate" is derived from the Persian "shāh māt" ("the king is dead").

The oldest archaeological chess artifacts—ivory pieces—were excavated in ancient Afrasiab in Uzbekistan. They date to about 760 with some of them possibly being older. Almost all of the oldest pieces come from along the Silk Road. They have been found in the Tarim Basin (today's Xinjiang in China), Transoxiana, Sogdiana, Bactria, and Gandhara. That includes Iran on one end and India through Kashmir on the other. The game reached Western Europe and Russia via at least three routes. The earliest route was in the 9th century. By 1000, chess had spread throughout Muslim Iberia and Latin Europe. A 10th-century Latin poem called "Verses on Chess" is on display in Switzerland. A famous 13th-century Spanish book includes chess, backgammon, and dice. It is known as the Libro de los juegos and is the earliest European treatise on chess and table games. The rules were similar to those of the Arabic “shatranj.”
